content:
Quick answer: Personal Independence Payment (PIP) is a non-means-tested UK benefit for people aged 16 to State Pension age whose long-term condition substantially affects daily living and/or mobility. Arthritis can qualify when flares, stiffness, fatigue or aids change how you cook, wash, dress, move or plan journeys — not because of the diagnosis name alone. Start a claim via GOV.UK / DWP, describe your worst typical days, gather clinical evidence, and get free form help from Citizens Advice or a welfare rights service where you can.

This page is for people with arthritis and carers in the United Kingdom who need a clear map of PIP — not a promise of an award. Rules and rates change; always check the current GOV.UK guidance and take personal advice from a welfare adviser if your situation is complex (Scotland’s Adult Disability Payment has a different pathway).

For the wider benefits landscape see our Benefits & PIP hub. Newly diagnosed and still finding your feet? Start at newly diagnosed. Pain pacing sits in the pain-relief guide. If work is the pressure point, also read Access to Work.

What PIP is (and is not)

PIP has two components — Daily Living and Mobility — each with a standard and an enhanced rate. You can receive one or both. It is not means-tested and is not based solely on your arthritis type (OA, RA, PsA, AS and others can all be relevant when functional impact is high enough).

  • Daily Living looks at activities such as preparing food, eating, managing treatments, washing, dressing, communicating and engaging with other people.
  • Mobility looks at planning and following journeys, and moving around.

Assessors score descriptors. Aids, prompting and the reliability test (safely, repeatedly, to an acceptable standard, in a reasonable time) matter as much as “can you do it once on a good day”.

Eligibility signals that matter for arthritis

  • Morning stiffness that delays washing, dressing or leaving the house.
  • Flare days when grip, stairs, standing to cook or carrying shopping fail.
  • Fatigue after small tasks — how often you need to rest or get help.
  • Aids you already use (perching stool, jar openers, sticks, rails) and why.
  • Variability — worst typical days count; do not only describe your best week.

How to apply (England, Wales, Northern Ireland)

  1. Start the claim online or by phone via the current GOV.UK PIP claim route (DWP).
  2. Complete the “How your disability affects you” form — use concrete examples from a 2–4 week diary.
  3. Send supporting evidence: clinic letters, medication lists, OT/physio notes, flare diaries.
  4. Attend the assessment (telephone, video or face-to-face) if invited — answer for typical bad days.

In Scotland, new claims usually go through Adult Disability Payment rather than PIP — check Social Security Scotland guidance.

Tips that improve clarity (not “hacks”)

  • Write what happens on a bad but typical day, how long tasks take, and what goes wrong without help.
  • Name every joint that affects the activity (hands for buttons, knees for stairs, spine for washing hair).
  • Ask your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist for a short functional letter if they can.
  • Use Citizens Advice, local authority welfare rights or disability charities for free form checks.

If you disagree with the decision

You can usually ask for a mandatory reconsideration within the time limit on your decision letter, then appeal to a tribunal if needed. Many people succeed at appeal with clearer evidence — that is not a guarantee. Get advice early; deadlines are short.

PIP alongside work and other support

PIP can sit beside work. For workplace equipment and travel-to-work help, explore Access to Work and Equality Act reasonable adjustments. Food patterns that support energy are covered on the diet hub — diet does not replace benefits advice.

Quick questions

Does a diagnosis of arthritis automatically mean PIP? No. Awards turn on functional impact against the descriptors.

Should I apply on a good day? Describe your difficulties reliably across time, including flares — not only the hour you feel strongest.

Is this legal advice? No. It is educational information for UK readers. Confirm current rules on GOV.UK and with a welfare adviser.
